paragraphs.text: Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo, Fiona, dead at 9 years old
Fiona, the beloved 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus, has died after ingesting a knit hat that fell into her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo last week.
Her many fans had been following her treatment, which included medication, a colonoscopy and time on a vibration plate, through updates posted by the zoo.
“We are in shock at the moment,” zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”

Born six weeks premature in 2017 at just 29 pounds — normal birth weight, her keepers said, ranges from 55 to 120 pounds — she became an internet sensation as the zoo documented her growth and progress online. Her first birthday celebration, for which she was served a tower of tropical fruits, was broadcast to thousands of fans on Facebook Live.
The hat was flung into her habitat accidentally, the zoo said. There had been no sign that it had passed through her digestive system and out of her body.
Fiona was initially asymptomatic, the zoo said, but within a few days her appetite started to decline. She was sedated, examined and given medications, but the hat was not retrieved.

She was sedated again this week, the zoo said, for an evaluation that included a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. She was given fluids and medications to help her pass the hat. She was also given her favorite foods to encourage digestion.
On Wednesday, zoo staff members encouraged her to stand on a vibration plate borrowed from a nearby horse farm to help move the hat through her intestines.

Surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, the zoo said. Veterinary staff members tried everything they could to help her, the zoo said. “Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.”
“The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo said.
Before Fiona’s death was announced, the news station WCPO reported Thursday that students at local schools were making get-well cards for her.
